The pre-test version is correct, and the general rule it illustrates is the one the course's own flowchart hides: a post-test loop runs its body at least once, so it is safe only when the body must always execute at least once. Any loop whose correct number of repetitions may be zero - read N items, process a possibly empty list, consume input up to a sentinel that may come first - must test before the body.

questions.q: Compare i <- 1 ; WHILE i <= n with i <- 0 ; WHILE i < n and with i <- 1 ; WHILE i < n, each incrementing i by 1 at the end of the body. State how many times each body runs. Then explain when the choice between the first two genuinely matters even though the counts agree, and give the single value of n that most cheaply exposes the third as an off-by-one.
questions.concept: loop bounds and off-by-one
questions.why: i <- 1 ; WHILE i <= n runs the body n times, with i taking 1, 2, ..., n. i <- 0 ; WHILE i < n also runs the body n times, with i taking 0, 1, ..., n-1. i <- 1 ; WHILE i < n runs the body n-1 times, with i taking 1, 2, ..., n-1, one pass short. The rule to carry is that the number of passes is the start value, the test and the step taken together, never the constant in the test on its own. The first two agree on the COUNT but not on the VALUES i holds, and that is where the choice genuinely matters: whenever the body uses i rather than merely counting with it. Summing i gives n(n+1)/2 in the first and n(n-1)/2 in the second; multiplying by i makes the second start with a factor of 0; and using i as a position (the i-th number, the i-th item) hits a position 0 that may not exist, or misses the last one, depending on where positions are taken to begin. Pure counters are interchangeable; indices and accumulators are not. The cheapest test for the third loop is n = 1: i <- 1 ; WHILE i < 1 fails at once and the body never runs, so a task that should have been done once is not done at all - a one-line, one-input test that any larger n disguises, because at n = 10 the loop still runs nine times and looks busy and plausible.

recapCandidates.topic: The limit and the function value are two separate readings
recapCandidates.whyMisunderstood: Every earlier year of maths trains one reflex - to find the value at x = a, put a in - and this week's material exists to break it. Reading limits off a graph makes the split visible: the limit is about the height the curve heads towards as you slide in from each side, and f(a) is a single dot sitting on the vertical line x = a. They usually agree, which is why students never notice they are different questions, and then a hole or a jump appears and the reading collapses. Four errors follow. First, students read the x-value rather than the height: asked for the limit as x -> 2 they answer 2. Second, they read the plotted endpoint instead of the trend - at an open circle at (2, 5) the limit is 5, because the circle marks where the curve is heading even though the point itself is missing. Third, they think a discontinuity means the limit fails; at a removable discontinuity the limit exists perfectly well and it is f(a) that is missing or misplaced, and only a jump or an infinite discontinuity actually kills it. Fourth, they treat 'limit = infinity' as an answer of the same kind as 'limit = 3', when it is a description of how the limit fails to exist. Behind all four is a habit of reading a graph as a picture rather than as two independent measurements - one taken by approaching, one taken by landing.
whyQuestions: Why is the limit as x -> 2 a statement about the height the curve approaches and never about the number 2 itself?
Why does an open circle at (2, 5) with the curve running into it from both sides give a limit of 5, even though f(2) is not 5 and may not exist?
Why can a function have a perfectly good limit at a point where it is discontinuous, and which of the three continuity conditions is the one that fails there?
Why does a jump discontinuity destroy the two-sided limit while a removable one does not - what exactly is different about the two pictures?
Why is writing 'the limit as x -> 3 is plus infinity' not the same kind of answer as 'the limit is 7', and what is it actually telling you about the graph?
recapCandidates.goodAnswerContains: Separates the two readings explicitly: the limit is found by sliding in along the curve from the left and from the right and reading the y-height each side heads for, deliberately ignoring x = a; f(a) is read from the filled dot on the line x = a, and an open circle means no point there. States the existence test - the limit exists exactly when the two one-sided limits exist and are equal - and the three conditions for continuity at c: f(c) defined, the limit exists, and the two are equal. Classifies the failures by picture: removable (limit exists, f(c) missing or displaced, a hole); jump (one-sided limits both exist but differ); infinite (a one-sided limit runs off to plus or minus infinity, a vertical asymptote); and notes that '= infinity' records how the limit failed rather than supplying a value.
recapCandidates.workedExample: One graph, read four times. Take f so that: for x < 1 the curve rises smoothly to an open circle at (1, 3); a filled dot sits alone at (1, 5); for x > 1 the curve restarts at an open circle at (1, 3) and continues upward. At x = 4 the curve comes in from the left to a filled dot at (4, 2) and restarts on the right at an open circle at (4, 6). Near x = 7 it runs off to plus infinity on both sides. At x = 1: both one-sided limits are 3, so the limit is 3, but f(1) = 5. Conditions (i) and (ii) hold and (iii) fails, so this is a removable discontinuity - redefining f(1) = 3 repairs it, which is what removable means. At x = 4: the left limit is 2 and the right limit is 6, so the limit does not exist - a jump discontinuity. Note f(4) = 2 IS defined; a defined value does not rescue the limit, and here condition (ii) is the one that fails. At x = 7: both sides run to plus infinity, so we write the limit as plus infinity to describe the vertical asymptote, but it does not exist as a number and f(7) is undefined - an infinite discontinuity failing (i) and (ii). The contrast worth saying out loud: at x = 1 the limit exists and the function value is wrong; at x = 4 the function value exists and the limit is wrong. Two different failures, two different repairs, and no way to tell them apart if you only ever substitute.

recapCandidates.topic: The electric dipole in a uniform field - zero net force, non-zero torque
recapCandidates.whyMisunderstood: Students carry over one rule from mechanics - no net force means nothing happens - and a dipole in a uniform field breaks it visibly: the forces on +q and -q are equal and opposite so they cancel exactly and the centre of mass does not accelerate, yet the dipole turns. The reason is that the two forces do not act at the same point: they form a couple, and a couple has zero resultant but non-zero torque. A student who has only ever computed the sum of forces concludes the dipole is in equilibrium, which is wrong in the one way the exam always tests. The second trap is the direction of p: physics defines it from -q to +q, chemistry the other way, so mixing conventions reverses the sign of U = -p.E and predicts that alignment is the high-energy state. The third is reading the minus sign in U = -pE cos(theta) as decoration rather than physics - it is what makes theta = 0 (aligned, U = -pE) the stable minimum and theta = 180 (anti-aligned, U = +pE) the unstable maximum. The fourth is forgetting the word uniform: the cancellation depends on both charges feeling the same E, so in a non-uniform field there is a net force as well as a torque, which is why a charged rod attracts neutral paper. The fifth is the sin(theta) factor: torque is maximum at 90 degrees, not at 0, which is the opposite of what students guess.
whyQuestions: Why is the net force on a dipole in a uniform field exactly zero, and why does the dipole nevertheless rotate?
Why is the torque pE sin(theta) largest when the dipole is perpendicular to the field and zero when it is aligned or anti-aligned?
Why does U = -p.E carry a minus sign, and why does that make the aligned position a minimum of energy rather than a maximum?
Why are theta = 0 and theta = 180 both positions of zero torque, and yet only one of them a stable equilibrium - what test tells them apart?
Why does a charged plastic comb attract small neutral scraps of paper, given that the paper has no net charge and a dipole in a uniform field feels no net force?
recapCandidates.goodAnswerContains: Defines the dipole and its moment: charges +q and -q separated by d, with p = qd a vector of unit C.m pointing from -q to +q; and states that in a uniform field the two forces are +qE and -qE, equal and opposite, so the net force is zero. Explains the couple: the forces act at points separated by d, so they exert a torque pE sin(theta) (vector form p cross E), maximal at 90 degrees, zero at 0 and 180, always in the sense that rotates p towards E. Uses the energy to sort the equilibria: U = -pE cos(theta), so U(0) = -pE is the stable minimum (a nudge is pushed back), U(90) = 0, and U(180) = +pE is the unstable maximum; and notes that in a non-uniform field the cancellation fails and there is a net force towards the stronger field.
recapCandidates.workedExample: A dipole of charges plus and minus 2.0 nC separated by 3.0 mm sits in a uniform field E = 5.0 x 10^4 N/C at 30 degrees to the field. Dipole moment p = qd = (2.0 x 10^-9)(3.0 x 10^-3) = 6.0 x 10^-12 C.m. Net force: each charge feels qE = 1.0 x 10^-4 N, one along +E and one along -E, so the net force is zero and the dipole does not translate. Torque: pE sin(30) = (6.0 x 10^-12)(5.0 x 10^4)(0.50) = 1.5 x 10^-7 N.m, rotating p towards E; at 90 degrees the same dipole would feel 3.0 x 10^-7 N.m, the maximum, and at 0 or 180 degrees zero. Potential energy: U = -pE cos(30) = -2.6 x 10^-7 J. Work to reverse p (30 degrees to 210 degrees): U(210) = +2.6 x 10^-7 J, so W = 5.2 x 10^-7 J must be done against the field; rotating from 0 to 180 instead would cost the full 2pE = 6.0 x 10^-7 J, the largest possible, from the stable minimum to the unstable maximum. The paper scrap: the comb's field is non-uniform, strongest near the comb, and induces a dipole in the paper with the near end oppositely charged; the near end sits in a stronger field than the far end, so the forces no longer cancel and there is a net pull towards the comb. Uniformity, not neutrality, is what made the net force vanish in the first place.
